title: Proxy Pattern
tagline: Place a placeholder in front of a real object to control access, add lazy loading, cache results, or enforce security — transparently.

sections.content:
Imagine every time a user opens your web app, the system immediately creates and connects to every service it might ever need — a heavy image processor, a remote payment gateway, an AI inference engine — even when the user just wants to log in. That is expensive, slow, and wasteful. Or imagine sprinkling `if (!user.isAdmin) return;` checks in ten different methods across your codebase to protect a sensitive service. That is fragile, repetitive, and a maintenance nightmare.

**The Proxy pattern** is the GoF structural solution to both problems: you place a lightweight stand-in object — a *proxy* — in front of the real object. The proxy implements the exact same interface as the real object, so callers cannot tell the difference. Internally, the proxy intercepts each method call and decides: should I create the real object now? Should I check permissions first? Can I return a cached result without touching the real object at all? Should I forward this call over the network to a remote service?

**Why this matters in practice:** Every major framework and runtime uses the Proxy pattern under the hood. Vue 3's entire reactivity system is built on JavaScript's language-level `Proxy` object. Hibernate and JPA lazy-load database relationships using virtual proxies. gRPC and SOAP generate client stubs that are remote proxies. Service workers in browsers are network-level proxies. Understanding the pattern gives you the mental model to reason about all of these systems at once.

**Four canonical proxy variants:**
- **Virtual Proxy** — defers expensive object creation until the first real need (lazy initialisation).
- **Protection Proxy** — enforces access control before forwarding calls, keeping auth out of business logic.
- **Caching Proxy** — stores results of expensive operations and short-circuits repeat calls.
- **Remote Proxy** — represents an object living in a different process or machine, handling serialisation transparently.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to implement all four variants in JavaScript, recognise them in real framework source code, and know precisely when the pattern adds value versus when it adds noise.

sections.caption: The Client depends only on the Subject interface — it is oblivious to whether it is talking to a Proxy or to the RealSubject directly. The Proxy holds a reference to the RealSubject and intercepts every call.

sections.title: The Bank Teller, the Spokesperson, and the CDN
sections.content:
**Bank teller (Protection Proxy):** You walk into a bank and ask to withdraw money from the vault. You do not walk into the vault yourself. The teller is the proxy: they check your ID, verify your balance and daily limit, and only then retrieve your money from the vault (the real object) on your behalf. The vault never knows who you are — authentication lives in the teller. This is a *protection proxy*.

**Corporate spokesperson (Remote Proxy):** At a press conference, journalists ask questions to the CEO's spokesperson. The spokesperson listens, relays to the CEO (possibly in another building), gets an answer, and responds. From the journalist's perspective, they are talking to someone who can answer their questions — the fact that the real decision-maker is elsewhere is transparent. This is a *remote proxy*.

**CDN edge node (Caching Proxy):** When you request a popular image from a website, you often do not reach the origin server at all. A content delivery network node geographically near you holds a cached copy and serves it instantly. The CDN is a proxy: if it has the content (cache hit), it serves directly; if not (cache miss), it fetches from the origin, stores the result, and responds. This is a *caching proxy*.

All three examples share the same structure: a stand-in that implements the same contract as the real thing, intercepting calls to add value — security, location transparency, or speed.

sections.title: The Four Participants — Roles and Responsibilities
sections.content:
**Subject Interface** defines the contract that both the real object and the proxy honour. This shared interface is what makes the proxy transparent — the client codes against an abstraction and genuinely cannot distinguish a proxy from the real thing. In JavaScript this is a shared class with abstract methods, or simply a duck-typed agreement on method names.

**Real Subject** is the actual object that performs meaningful work. It is expensive (heavy computation, I/O), sensitive (requires permissions), or remote (lives on another machine). Crucially, the Real Subject does *not* know it is being proxied — it has no proxy-specific code.

**Proxy** holds a reference to the Real Subject (or creates it on demand). It implements the Subject interface so the client can use it interchangeably. Before (and sometimes after) delegating to the Real Subject, it performs its cross-cutting concern: lazy initialisation, permission checks, cache lookups, logging, or network serialisation. Multiple proxy types can even be chained — a protection proxy wrapping a caching proxy wrapping a remote proxy, each layer ignorant of the others.

**Client** holds a reference typed to the Subject interface. It calls methods and receives results without caring whether those calls hit a proxy or the real object directly. This ignorance is what lets you introduce or remove proxies without changing client code — a huge maintenance win.

**Key structural insight:** The Proxy and the RealSubject implement the same interface. This is not optional — it is the mechanism by which transparency is achieved. Anything the client can do with a RealSubject it can do with a Proxy. Liskov Substitution Principle in practice.

sections.title: Virtual Proxy — Lazy Initialisation in Depth
sections.content:
A Virtual Proxy defers the creation of a **heavyweight object** until the moment it is first truly needed. The proxy holds `null` for the real object reference. On the first method call that requires the real object, the proxy instantiates it, stores the reference, and delegates. Every subsequent call reuses the already-initialised object — so the cost is paid exactly once and only when necessary.

**When does this matter?** Consider an ORM relationship: a `User` entity has a `orders` collection that could contain thousands of records. Loading all orders every time you fetch a user is wasteful — most callers only want the user's name and email. The ORM creates a virtual proxy for `user.orders`. Reading `user.name` never touches the database again. Only when code actually iterates `user.orders` does the ORM fire a `SELECT` query. This is Hibernate's `PersistentBag` in action.

**The subtle power of partial answers:** A Virtual Proxy can answer some queries without initialising the real object at all. If the proxy stores the filename but not the image data, `getSize()` can return 0 (or a stored metadata value) without loading the binary data. Only `display()` needs the real load. This is an optimisation on top of the lazy init — serve cheap information cheaply.

**Initialisation timing is critical:** If the constructor of the Real Subject has side effects (fires events, acquires a lock, opens a file handle), then the timing of those side effects shifts from 'when you create the proxy' to 'when you first call a method'. This can be a benefit (eager locking avoided) or a bug (a lock is acquired mid-request unexpectedly). Document and test the timing behaviour.

**Thread safety warning:** In multithreaded environments (Node.js worker threads, Java, Go), the `if (!this._real) this._real = new RealSubject()` check is a classic double-checked locking scenario. Without synchronisation, two threads might both see `_real === null` and both create a RealSubject, causing duplicate initialisation, resource leaks, or corrupted state. Use a mutex, a promise cache, or atomic compare-and-set depending on your runtime.

sections.title: Protection Proxy — Access Control Without Pollution
sections.content:
A Protection Proxy enforces access control **before** forwarding calls to the Real Subject. The Real Subject never contains a single `if (!user.hasPermission...)` line — that concern lives entirely in the proxy layer. The benefits compound:

**Single point of enforcement:** Authorization logic is in one file. When rules change (new roles, new endpoints), you change one proxy class, not every method in every service.

**Testability:** You can test the Real Subject with full access (no proxy) and test the proxy independently with mocked subjects and various user fixtures. The concerns are cleanly separated.

**Gradual introduction:** You can add a protection proxy to an existing service without touching the service code. Wrap it at the composition root (dependency injection container), and every caller gets access control for free.

**Layered policies:** A proxy can enforce coarse-grained role checks, while the Real Subject enforces fine-grained business rules. Or stack two proxies — a rate-limiting proxy outside a permission-checking proxy — each handling one concern.

**What it is NOT:** A protection proxy is not a replacement for server-side auth in a networked system. If a caller can bypass the proxy and call the Real Subject directly (e.g., by importing the class and calling it), the protection is meaningless. The proxy pattern provides in-process architectural separation of concerns. Network-level security requires network-level solutions (API gateways, mTLS, firewalls) in addition.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three proxies, one pattern: the ImageProxy defers expensive disk I/O and can answer `getSize()` cheaply before the real image loads. The SecureDocumentProxy centralises all permission checks in `_require()` — DocumentService has zero auth code. The CachingWeatherProxy uses a TTL-aware Map to avoid hammering the live service — a pattern identical to what Redis does at the infrastructure level.

sections.title: Caching Proxy — Design Decisions and Pitfalls
sections.content:
A caching proxy is straightforward to write but has several important design decisions that distinguish a production-ready implementation from a toy:

**Cache key design:** The key must uniquely identify the combination of inputs that determines the output. For a single string argument (`city`), the string is the key. For complex objects, you may need to serialize to JSON or use a hash. A wrong key (too coarse) causes cache collisions; too fine means you never get cache hits.

**Expiry and invalidation:** Pure in-memory caches without expiry grow forever and serve stale data. Options include TTL (time-to-live) per entry, LRU (least recently used) eviction, and explicit invalidation when the underlying data changes. Cache invalidation is famously one of the hardest problems in computer science — 'there are only two hard things: cache invalidation and naming things.'

**Cache stampede (thundering herd):** If the cache expires and ten concurrent requests simultaneously detect a miss, all ten will simultaneously call the expensive real service. The solution is a *single-flight* pattern: track in-progress requests by key and return the same promise to all concurrent callers. The real service is called exactly once.

**Mutable vs. immutable results:** If the returned objects are mutable, callers modifying the returned object will corrupt the cached copy. Either return deep clones, freeze the cached object (`Object.freeze`), or document that results are read-only.

**Cache invalidation strategies:**
- **Write-through**: update cache synchronously when data changes (consistent, slower writes)
- **Write-around**: invalidate cache on write, re-populate on next read (simpler, brief stale window)
- **Write-behind**: update cache immediately, queue the real write asynchronously (fast, risk of data loss on crash)

For most application-level caching proxies, write-around with TTL is the pragmatic choice.

sections.title: Remote Proxy — Transparent Network Calls
sections.content:
A Remote Proxy makes a **distant object** appear local. The client calls methods as if the object is in the same process; the proxy transparently serialises the call, sends it over a network, receives the response, and deserialises it back. This pattern is the foundation of every RPC (Remote Procedure Call) framework ever built.

**How it works in practice:**
1. A code generator (protoc for gRPC, wsdl2java for SOAP) reads a service definition and emits a client stub class.
2. The stub implements the same interface as the service.
3. The client uses the stub as if it were local.
4. Internally, the stub serialises method arguments to bytes (Protobuf, JSON, XML), opens a connection (HTTP/2, HTTP/1.1), sends the payload, waits for the response, and deserialises it.

**gRPC stub example:** `const client = new UserServiceClient('localhost:50051', grpc.credentials.createInsecure())`. Then `client.getUser({ id: 42 }, callback)` looks like a local method call but goes over the wire. The stub IS the remote proxy.

**Differences from other proxies:**
- Remote proxies must handle **network failures** (timeouts, connection errors, retries) that local proxies never face.
- They must handle **latency** — calls are not synchronous from a wall-clock perspective even if the API is synchronous.
- They involve **serialisation** — not all types survive the round-trip (object identity, circular references, function references are lost).
- They often implement **service discovery** — knowing which host and port to connect to, with load balancing across multiple instances.

**Service workers as browser-level remote proxies:** A service worker intercepts HTTP fetch events from the main page (the client) and decides: serve from cache, forward to network, or return a custom response. The page code calls `fetch('/api/data')` exactly the same whether a service worker is registered or not — the service worker is a transparent proxy at the HTTP level.

sections.mermaid:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as "Client (Browser)"
    participant SW as "Service Worker\n(Remote Proxy)"
    participant N as "Network / Server"
    C->>SW: fetch('/api/data')
    SW->>SW: Check cache
    alt "Cached and fresh"
        SW-->>C: Return cached response
    else "Cache miss"
        SW->>N: Forward request
        N-->>SW: Response
        SW->>SW: Update cache
        SW-->>C: Return response
    end
sections.caption: Service workers are browser-level remote proxies. The page's `fetch()` calls are intercepted transparently — the page code is unchanged regardless of whether a service worker is active.

sections.title: JavaScript's Built-in Proxy — Language-Level Interception
sections.content:
ES6 introduced `new Proxy(target, handler)`, a language primitive that lets you intercept nearly any operation on an object. Unlike the classic GoF class-based proxy, the ES6 Proxy does not require you to implement a shared interface — it works on any object, including existing ones, and intercepts operations at the engine level.

**Available traps** (the operations you can intercept):
- `get(target, prop, receiver)` — property read: `obj.x`
- `set(target, prop, value, receiver)` — property write: `obj.x = 5`
- `has(target, prop)` — `in` operator: `'x' in obj`
- `deleteProperty(target, prop)` — `delete obj.x`
- `apply(target, thisArg, args)` — function call: `fn(1, 2)` (target must be a function)
- `construct(target, args)` — `new Constructor(...)`
- `ownKeys(target)` — `Object.keys()`, `for...in`
- `getOwnPropertyDescriptor`, `defineProperty`, `getPrototypeOf`, `setPrototypeOf`, and more

**Vue 3 reactivity:** Vue 3 rewrote its reactivity system using `Proxy` (replacing Vue 2's `Object.defineProperty`). When you call `reactive({ count: 0 })`, Vue wraps the object in a Proxy. The `get` trap tracks which effect (render function, computed property) read `count` — this is *dependency tracking*. The `set` trap notifies all dependent effects that `count` changed — this is *triggering updates*. The entire reactivity system is a caching/notification proxy built on ES6 `Proxy`.

**MobX observables:** Similarly, MobX wraps your state objects in ES6 Proxies. Accessing a property inside a `reaction` or `autorun` records the dependency; mutation triggers re-runs.

**Validation proxies:** A common pattern is wrapping a configuration object in a Proxy that validates values in the `set` trap — reject invalid types or out-of-range values before they reach the object.

**Revocable proxies:** `Proxy.revocable(target, handler)` returns a `{ proxy, revoke }` pair. After calling `revoke()`, any operation on the proxy throws a TypeError. This is used for security — a capability can be granted and then permanently revoked.

**Performance note:** ES6 Proxy traps have overhead compared to direct property access. For hot paths (tight loops reading the same property millions of times per second), avoid proxied objects. Vue mitigates this by tracking which properties were accessed and caching that information, only re-running proxy overhead when necessary.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Three ES6 Proxy use-cases in 80 lines: (1) the validation proxy catches bad config values at the point of assignment, turning silent bugs into immediate errors; (2) the revocable proxy shows how capabilities can be permanently withdrawn — used in secure sandboxing; (3) the mini-reactivity system is structurally identical to Vue 3's core: `get` tracks which effects depend on which properties, `set` notifies them when values change.

sections.title: Proxy vs. Decorator — The Intent Distinction
sections.content:
The Proxy and Decorator patterns are structurally nearly identical: both wrap an object, both implement the same interface as the wrapped object, both forward calls. This causes frequent confusion — including in some textbooks. The distinction is **intent**, and intent drives when you reach for each.

**Proxy — controls access to the real object.** The proxy manages the *relationship* between the client and the real object: it decides if and when the real object is created, whether the call is allowed, whether a cached result can substitute, or how the call should be forwarded remotely. The existence of the real object (and the nature of the call) determines what the proxy does. The proxy is often transparent — the client does not know there is a proxy.

**Decorator — adds behaviour to the real object.** The decorator extends what the real object *does*: it might add logging before/after a call, wrap results, add retry logic, or compose additional operations. The decorator always delegates to the wrapped object; the question is not *whether* to delegate but *what additional work* to do around delegation. Decorators are often stacked intentionally — `new LoggingDecorator(new RetryDecorator(new RealService()))`.

**The practical test:** Ask 'does the wrapper control whether/when the real object is called, or does it augment what happens around the call?' Control → Proxy. Augment → Decorator.

**Proxy vs. Facade:** A Facade simplifies a complex subsystem behind a single interface, without necessarily implementing the same interface. A Proxy implements the same interface as one specific class and intercepts its calls. Different scope.

**Proxy vs. Adapter:** An Adapter converts one interface to another (impedance matching). A Proxy keeps the same interface and adds cross-cutting behaviour. If the interface changes, it is an Adapter; if the interface stays the same, it is a Proxy.

**Proxy vs. Middleware (in web frameworks):** Express/Koa middleware pipelines are a Proxy-like pattern at the request/response level: each middleware intercepts the call, optionally modifies it, optionally delegates to the next layer, optionally post-processes the response. The structural similarity is not coincidence — both are about intercepting and controlling a call pipeline.

flowchart LR

    D["Client"] --> E["Decorator\n(same interface)"] --> F["RealObject"]
    G["Client"] --> H["Adapter\n(different interface)"] --> I["Adaptee"]

sections.caption: Three structural patterns that all involve wrapping: Proxy controls access (same interface), Decorator adds behaviour (same interface), Adapter converts interface (different interface). Intent separates them.

sections.title: Real-World Framework Usage and Advanced Patterns
sections.content:
Understanding where the Proxy pattern appears in real frameworks lets you read unfamiliar code faster and make better design decisions:

**Hibernate / JPA lazy loading:** When you fetch a `User` entity with a `@OneToMany orders` relationship, Hibernate does not load the orders immediately. Instead, `user.getOrders()` returns a `PersistentBag` — a virtual proxy. It appears to be a normal `List<Order>` (same interface), but the first call that iterates it fires a SQL query. If you serialise the User to JSON outside a transaction (common in Spring controllers), you hit the infamous `LazyInitializationException` — the proxy tries to load data but the database session is already closed. This is a direct consequence of the Virtual Proxy pattern.

**Vue 3 Reactivity:** As shown above, `reactive()` returns an ES6 Proxy. The `ref()` function wraps a primitive in a reactive object with a `.value` accessor — same proxy concept, different surface area. The reactive compiler (`@vue/compiler-dom`) can even compile away the `.value` unwrapping at build time, making refs feel like plain variables in `<script setup>`. The entire DX is built on the Proxy pattern.

**Node.js `http-proxy` and nginx:** nginx in reverse-proxy mode intercepts HTTP requests, applies SSL termination, load balancing, and rate limiting, then forwards to upstream services. It is a remote proxy + caching proxy + protection proxy combined in a single infrastructure component.

**Jest `spyOn`:** `jest.spyOn(obj, 'method')` replaces `obj.method` with a proxy that records calls and (optionally) modifies return values, then delegates to the original. This is a protection/logging proxy for testing.

**Python `__getattr__` and `__setattr__`:** Python's magic methods allow the same proxy pattern without ES6 `Proxy`. SQLAlchemy's lazy-loaded column data, dataclasses, and attrs all use `__getattr__` to intercept attribute access.

**Proxy chains (composing proxies):** You can stack proxies — each wrapping the next — to compose multiple cross-cutting concerns:
```
const proxy = new LoggingProxy(
  new CachingProxy(
    new SecureProxy(
      new RealService(), currentUser
    )
  )
);
```
Each proxy layer is unaware of the others. The request flows: Logging → Caching (cache hit? return early) → Security (check permissions) → RealService. This is structurally similar to middleware pipelines and aspect-oriented programming.

**Historical context:** The term 'proxy' in computing predates the GoF book by decades — it was first used in the context of remote procedure calls in the 1970s (the 'stub' in Sun RPC). The GoF formalised it in 1994 as one of the original 23 design patterns. JavaScript's `Proxy` object was proposed in the ES Harmony specification around 2010 and reached ES6 in 2015. It was one of the most requested JavaScript features because reactive UI frameworks (AngularJS, Backbone, Knockout) were all building their own property-interception hacks using `Object.defineProperty`, and a language-level solution was desperately needed. Vue 2 used `Object.defineProperty`; Vue 3 switched to `Proxy` and as a result works with arrays and dynamically added properties without any special handling.

**When to use the Proxy pattern:**
- You have an **expensive object** (heavy I/O, network call, large allocation) and want to defer creation until first use — reach for Virtual Proxy.
- You need **access control** on a service without polluting the service with auth code — reach for Protection Proxy.
- You have an **expensive read** that is called frequently with the same arguments — reach for Caching Proxy with a TTL.
- You need to make a **remote service** look like a local object — reach for Remote Proxy (or use a framework that generates stubs).
- You need to **intercept arbitrary operations** on an existing object (Vue reactivity, validation, logging) — reach for ES6 `new Proxy()`.

**When NOT to use it:**
- When the proxy **adds no logic** — a class that only does `return this._real.method()` is indirection without value; delete it.
- When the additional layer makes **debugging significantly harder** without a compensating benefit — proxies can obscure stack traces and make 'go to definition' confusing.
- When **performance is critical** in a hot path — ES6 `Proxy` traps have measurable overhead on tight loops.
- When you could use **simpler language features** — a module that exports functions is often simpler than a class wrapped in a proxy for the same result.
- Do not confuse 'interesting pattern' with 'needed pattern'. Proxy is powerful; it is not universally appropriate.

**Gotchas:**
- Hibernate `LazyInitializationException` = proxy outlived its session. Load eagerly or use DTOs for serialisation.
- ES6 `Proxy` on frozen objects will throw in strict mode. Check `Object.isFrozen` before proxying.
- Circular proxy chains (proxy A wraps proxy B wraps proxy A) will stack-overflow on the first call.

items: The **Proxy pattern** places a stand-in object in front of a real object, implementing the same interface so callers are transparent to the substitution — this is the pattern's defining characteristic.

**Virtual Proxy** defers expensive object creation until first use; it can serve cheap partial answers (metadata, defaults) without ever touching the real object — Hibernate lazy loading is the canonical example.
**Protection Proxy** centralises access control in one class, keeping the Real Subject free of auth code; this upholds SRP and makes policy changes a one-file edit.
**Caching Proxy** short-circuits repeat calls by storing results; key design decisions are cache key structure, TTL, invalidation strategy, and the thundering-herd problem for concurrent misses.
**Remote Proxy** makes a networked object appear local by handling serialisation, transport, and error recovery transparently — gRPC stubs and service workers are real-world remote proxies.

**ES6 `new Proxy(target, handler)`** is a language-level Proxy with traps for `get`, `set`, `apply`, and more — Vue 3's reactivity system, MobX observables, and validation libraries are all built on it.

**Proxy vs. Decorator:** structurally similar but intent differs — Proxy *controls access* (if/when to call the real object); Decorator *adds behaviour* around delegation (always delegates, augments what happens).

quiz.question: What is the defining structural characteristic of the Proxy pattern that makes it transparent to the client?
options: The proxy inherits all private fields from the real object
The proxy implements the same interface as the real object so callers cannot distinguish them
The proxy always stores a deep clone of the real object
The proxy must be registered in a global registry before use
quiz.explanation: Interface transparency is what makes a Proxy a Proxy. By implementing the same interface as the Real Subject, the client can use the proxy wherever a real object is expected — without any code changes. This is the pattern's foundational mechanism.

quiz.question: Hibernate's `PersistentBag` (returned by `user.getOrders()`) is an example of which proxy variant, and what does it do?
options: Remote Proxy — it serialises the order list over the network
Virtual Proxy — it defers the SQL query until the collection is first iterated
Protection Proxy — it checks that the user has permission to read orders
Caching Proxy — it stores all orders in an in-memory map
quiz.explanation: Hibernate's lazy-loaded collections are Virtual Proxies. They implement the List interface but defer the SELECT query until the first method that requires real data (e.g., iteration, size). This is why accessing them outside an open session causes LazyInitializationException — the proxy tries to load from a closed database session.

quiz.question: In a Virtual Proxy for an expensive image, `getSize()` returns 0 before `display()` is called. Why is this architecturally acceptable?
options: It is not acceptable — the proxy must always load the real image to answer any query
The proxy can serve cheap partial answers without loading the expensive resource, deferring cost to when it is truly necessary
0 is always the correct size for unloaded images in this pattern
The client should know to call display() before getSize()
quiz.explanation: One power of the Virtual Proxy is serving cheap information cheaply. The proxy knows the filename (cheap) but not the binary data (expensive). If the caller only needs a placeholder size, returning 0 avoids an unnecessary I/O operation. This is a deliberate trade-off, not a bug — document the contract clearly.

quiz.question: A Protection Proxy keeps auth logic out of the Real Subject. Which SOLID principle does this most directly support?
options: Open/Closed Principle — the real subject is closed to modification
Single Responsibility Principle — business logic and access control are separate concerns in separate classes
Liskov Substitution Principle — the proxy is substitutable for the real subject
Interface Segregation Principle — auth is split into its own interface
quiz.explanation: SRP states a class should have one reason to change. By putting auth in the proxy, the Real Subject changes only when business logic changes, not when permission rules change. The proxy changes only when auth policy changes. Two classes, two reasons to change — clean separation.

quiz.question: What is the 'cache stampede' (thundering herd) problem in a Caching Proxy, and what is the standard mitigation?
options: The cache grows too large and crashes memory — mitigated by LRU eviction
Multiple concurrent requests all detect a cache miss simultaneously and all call the real service — mitigated by the single-flight pattern (deduplicate in-flight requests by key)
The cache returns stale data — mitigated by shorter TTLs
The cache key collides across different inputs — mitigated by hashing
quiz.explanation: When a cached entry expires under high load, many concurrent requests simultaneously see a miss and simultaneously call the expensive real service. Single-flight (also called request coalescing) tracks in-progress fetches by key and returns the same promise to all concurrent callers — the real service is called exactly once per cache miss.

quiz.question: Vue 3 uses ES6 `Proxy` for reactivity. What does the `get` trap specifically do in Vue's reactive system?
options: It prevents reading properties on non-reactive objects
It intercepts property reads to record which effects (render functions, computed) depend on that property — dependency tracking
It caches the property value to avoid repeated Vue internals computation
It converts raw values to Vue's internal observable format
quiz.explanation: Vue 3's `get` trap implements dependency tracking: when a render function or computed property reads a reactive property, Vue records that dependency. When the property later changes (set trap fires), Vue knows exactly which effects to re-run — this is the foundation of Vue's efficient update system.

quiz.question: What is a Revocable Proxy (`Proxy.revocable()`), and what is its primary use case?
options: A proxy that automatically revokes its cache entries after a TTL
A proxy whose access can be permanently withdrawn — used to grant and later revoke a capability for security sandboxing
A proxy that can only be used once before it must be recreated
A proxy that reverts all set operations when an error occurs
quiz.explanation: Proxy.revocable() returns a proxy and a revoke function. After revoke() is called, any operation on the proxy throws a TypeError — permanently. This is used in capability-based security: grant a third party a proxy to your data, then revoke it when their access period ends. No copy of the capability can be used after revocation.

quiz.question: What is the key intent distinction between the Proxy pattern and the Decorator pattern, given that both implement the same interface as the wrapped object?
options: Proxy uses class inheritance; Decorator uses object composition
Proxy controls access (if/when the real object is called); Decorator adds behaviour around delegation (always calls the wrapped object, augments what happens)
Proxy can only be used once; Decorator can be stacked multiple times
Proxy is a GoF pattern; Decorator is not recognised by GoF
quiz.explanation: Both patterns wrap an object and implement the same interface, so the structural distinction is minimal. Intent separates them: Proxy controls access — deciding whether to create the real object, whether to forward the call, or returning a cached result. Decorator always delegates to the wrapped object and adds behaviour around that delegation.

quiz.question: A gRPC client stub is which type of proxy, and what problem does it solve?
options: Virtual Proxy — it lazily connects to the gRPC server on first call
Protection Proxy — it checks client certificates before forwarding
Remote Proxy — it makes a service on another machine appear as a local method call by handling serialisation and network transport
Caching Proxy — it caches gRPC responses to reduce server load
quiz.explanation: gRPC stubs are Remote Proxies. They implement the same service interface as the server-side implementation but internally serialise arguments to Protobuf, send over HTTP/2, receive the response, and deserialise it. From the caller's perspective it looks like a local method call — network complexity is hidden behind the proxy.

quiz.question: When should you NOT use the Proxy pattern?
options: When you need lazy loading of a database-backed collection
When you need to enforce role-based access control on a service
When the proxy would only delegate every call with no added logic — adding indirection without value
When making a remote service appear local to callers
quiz.explanation: A proxy that only does `return this._real.method()` with no additional logic (no access control, no lazy init, no caching, no logging) adds a layer of indirection that makes code harder to navigate without providing any benefit. Apply the pattern only when there is genuine proxy work — interception, control, or augmentation — to be done.
